plants.location: Shared terracotta pot with the other split rock
plants.container: Terracotta pot, peat-based mix with perlite (too rich for a mesemb: see health steps)
plants.growth_habit: A stemless succulent of one or two pairs of thick, egg-shaped leaves; a new pair grows up through the cleft each year as the old pair shrivels
plants.temp_notes: Takes a light frost only when bone dry. Keep it above freezing; cool (45-55 F) and dry in winter is ideal.
plants.humidity_notes: Likes dry air. Damp, still air invites rot.
plants.light_summary: Full sun to very bright light
plants.light_notes: The brightest window you have, or a strong grow light close up. Too little light stretches the bodies, splits them early and loses the purple colour.
plants.winter_summary: A South African desert succulent: frost-tender when there is any moisture in the mix. Winter is its dry rest.
plants.winter_triggers: Indoors before any night under 40 F; no water from about November until the old leaves have fully shrivelled.
plants.winter_steps:
Keep it in the sunniest window, cool and completely dry.
Do not water when the body wrinkles in winter: it is drawing on the old leaves, which is normal.
Resume light watering in spring once the old pair has dried to paper.
plants.indoor_setup: South or west window, right against the glass, or a grow light 6-10 in away for 12-14 h a day. Dry air is fine; no pebble tray.
plants.water_notes: The main way to kill it is water. Water only when the body is wrinkled and the mix has been dry for a week, soak once, then nothing until it wrinkles again. Never water while a new pair of leaves is growing from the cleft (late winter to spring) or while the old pair is still plump.
plants.soil_medium: Very gritty: at least 70% pumice, coarse sand or fine gravel, 30% or less potting soil. The peat mix it is in now holds water far too long.
plants.fertilizer: Almost none: a quarter-strength cactus feed once or twice in the growing season, or none at all
plants.nutrients: Low nitrogen. Rich feeding makes soft, split bodies.
plants.pests_watch:
Mealybugs: white fluff in the cleft and at the base
Root mealybugs: white powder on the roots when repotting
Rot: a soft, translucent, brown body (from water, not a pest)
plants.pest_steps:
Look into the cleft with a torch every couple of weeks.
Dab mealybugs with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol.
A soft or mushy body cannot be saved; keep the pot bone dry to protect the other plant.
plants.zone_notes: Frost-tender in Round Rock: indoors from the first cold nights, dry.
plants.native_range: Great Karoo, Eastern Cape and Free State, South Africa: open, stony, semi-desert ground with summer and autumn rain.
plants.conservation_status: Least Concern (wild); the plant in the pot is nursery-grown.
plants.bloom: A large yellow-orange, daisy-like flower from the cleft in autumn or early winter, opening in the afternoon, on a mature plant.
plants.fruit: A seed capsule that opens when wet; rarely set indoors.
plants.danger_humans: Not known to be toxic. Not for eating.
plants.danger_animals: Not on the ASPCA toxic lists. Keep it out of reach anyway: a chewed body is a dead plant.
plants.propagation: Seed (easy, slow). Division of a clump of two or more heads in spring, letting the cut dry for a few days before potting.

Identified by Claude from the photos (85% sure for the purple one, 75% for the green) and confirmed by Pl@ntNet (96%). Ethan: the picture checker alone named six wrong plants; this was the case that led to 1.40.0.
plants.aliases: Split rock, living stone, purple split rock
plants.id_basis: An egg-shaped, speckled purple-pink body about 1.5 in long with a single deep cleft and the pink inner surfaces of the next leaf pair showing: Pleiospilos nelii, in the purple form sold as 'Royal Flush'. Pl@ntNet named the pot Pleiospilos nelii at 96% (Identify page, November 5). The fine dark dots and the domed, windowless top rule out Lithops; the size rules out Conophytum.
plants.id_alternatives:
Pleiospilos nelii, green form gone purple in strong sun
Pleiospilos compactus (longer, more pointed leaves)
Lithops (no: Lithops have flat, windowed tops)
plants.id_improve:
A photo of the flower, if it blooms (purple form: pink-purple; green form: yellow-orange)
A photo from directly above in daylight, with a ruler
plants.health_summary: Firm, well-coloured body with the new pair starting in the cleft. The mix is a peat-based potting soil with perlite, which holds far too much water for a mesemb.
plants.health_observations:
Body plump and firm, speckled purple
Next leaf pair visible in the cleft
Peat-based mix in a terracotta pot
plants.health_steps:
Repot both plants into a very gritty mix (mostly pumice or coarse sand) at the next dry spell, without watering for a week after.
No water at all until the body wrinkles.
Give it the sunniest spot in the house for the winter.

plants.aliases: Flat-leaved vanilla, Bourbon vanilla, vanilla vine
plants.container: Black nursery pot of sphagnum moss inside a light-blue cache pot, with a plastic-mesh moss pole
plants.growth_habit: A succulent-stemmed vine that climbs by aerial roots at each node, zigzagging up its support; reaches 20 ft or more with time
plants.id_basis: A thick, fleshy, zigzag green stem climbing a moss pole with a flat oblong leaf and a grey-green aerial root at every node, in sphagnum: the vanilla orchid, Vanilla planifolia (the species grown for vanilla pods). The leaf shape and the climbing habit with node roots are unmistakable among houseplants.
plants.id_alternatives:
Vanilla planifolia (plain green; variegated forms have cream edges)
Vanilla pompona (broader, larger leaves; rare in cultivation)
plants.id_improve:
A photo of a leaf from the side showing its thickness and the aerial root
Where it was bought
plants.temp_notes: Tropical: keep it above 60 F. Chilling below 50 F yellows and drops leaves.
plants.humidity_notes: Wants humid air; dry heated rooms brown the leaf tips and stall the aerial roots. Mist the moss pole, not the leaves.
plants.light_notes: Bright but not hot sun: an east window, or a few feet from a south one. Yellow, bleached leaves mean too much direct sun; long gaps between leaves mean too little light.
plants.winter_summary: A tropical orchid: indoors all year in Round Rock.
plants.winter_triggers: Already indoors; keep it away from cold windows and heater vents.
plants.winter_steps:
Keep it warm (above 60 F) and the light bright.
Water a little less from November to February, but never let the moss dry out completely.
Mist the moss pole so the aerial roots keep growing into it.
plants.indoor_setup: East window or a grow light 10-14 in away for 12 h a day; a humidifier or a grouped, humid corner. Keep the moss pole damp: the aerial roots feed the vine as it climbs.
plants.water_notes: Water when the sphagnum is nearly dry on top but still slightly damp below, roughly weekly in summer and every 10-14 days in winter. Soak the moss pole at the same time. Let it drain; never leave the pot standing in water.
plants.soil_medium: Sphagnum moss, or a fine orchid bark and sphagnum mix, in a pot with plenty of drainage.
plants.fertilizer: Balanced orchid feed at quarter strength with every other watering in the growing season
plants.nutrients: Light, frequent feeding. Flush the moss with plain water monthly.
plants.pests_watch:
Mealybugs: white fluff at the nodes and under leaves
Scale: brown bumps along the stem
Spider mites in dry air: fine stippling
plants.pest_steps:
Check the nodes and leaf undersides every two weeks.
Wipe mealybugs and scale off with rubbing alcohol on a cotton bud.
Raise the humidity if mites appear.
plants.height_pot: Climbs its support: 2 to 3 ft on this pole, 10 ft and more given room
plants.zone_notes: A houseplant here; frost kills it.
plants.native_range: Mexico and Central America, climbing trees in warm, humid forest.
plants.conservation_status: Wild populations are in decline (assessed as Endangered in Mexico); the plant in the pot is nursery-grown.
plants.bloom: Pale greenish-yellow orchid flowers, each open for one day, on vines several years old and 10 ft or more long. Hand-pollinate for pods.
plants.fruit: The vanilla pod: a long green bean that takes 9 months to ripen and months of curing after. Rare indoors.
plants.danger_humans: The sap can irritate skin; wash after pruning. Cured pods are the vanilla of the kitchen.
plants.danger_animals: Not on the ASPCA toxic lists.
plants.propagation: Stem cuttings of 3 or more nodes laid on damp sphagnum, the lowest node buried, kept warm and humid.
plants.sources:
Wikipedia: Vanilla planifolia | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanilla_planifolia
ASPCA toxic and non-toxic plants | https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/toxic-and-non-toxic-plants
plants.health_summary: Climbing well with plenty of new leaves and aerial roots into the pole, but one leaf is yellowing and one at the base has dried brown, and the lower vine looks thin.
plants.health_observations:
Good new growth at the top of the pole
One yellowing leaf, one dried brown leaf near the base
Aerial roots reaching into the moss pole
Sphagnum looks dry on top
plants.health_steps:
Cut off the dried leaf; leave the yellowing one until it drops.
Keep the moss pole damp so the aerial roots can take hold.
Raise the humidity around it for the winter.
Feed lightly from spring.

plants.aliases: Tag: H-E-B 'Philodendron Ring of Fire, Philodendron serratum'; also sold as Philodendron 'Henderson's Pride'
plants.location: Indoors, on the plant table under the grow light
plants.container: Light-blue pot in a saucer, chunky mix of lava rock, bark and gravel; H-E-B tag
plants.growth_habit: A slow, self-heading to short-climbing philodendron with long, narrow, saw-edged leaves that open cream, orange or pink and settle to green with cream and yellow patches
plants.id_basis: The H-E-B tag reads 'Philodendron Ring of Fire, Philodendron serratum', and the plant matches: long narrow leaves with jagged, saw-toothed edges, speckled and blotched with cream and yellow, new leaves flushed orange-pink, red leaf stalks. 'Ring of Fire' is a hybrid (usually given as Philodendron wendlandii x tortum); 'serratum' on the tag is a trade name, not a valid species.
plants.id_alternatives:
Philodendron 'Ring of Fire' (as tagged)
Philodendron 'Jungle Boogie' / 'Tiger Tooth' (the same saw edge without the variegation)
Philodendron 'Paraiso Verde' (variegated but smooth-edged)
plants.id_improve: Nothing needed: the tag and the leaves agree.
plants.temp_notes: Tropical: chilling under 50 F marks the leaves; frost kills.
plants.humidity_notes: Likes humid air; the variegated parts brown at the edges in dry heated rooms.
plants.light_summary: Bright indirect light (not the full sun the tag says)
plants.light_hours: 6-8 h bright indirect, or a grow light 12 h
plants.light_notes: The tag's 'full sun' is for outdoor nurseries in shade cloth; indoors, direct midday sun scorches the cream patches. Good light keeps the variegation; too little turns new leaves plain green.
plants.winter_summary: A tropical aroid: indoors all year in Round Rock, under the grow light in winter.
plants.winter_triggers: Already indoors; keep it above 60 F and away from the window glass on cold nights.
plants.winter_steps:
Keep it under the grow light 12 h a day.
Water less in winter: let the chunky mix dry almost through.
No feeding from November to February.
plants.indoor_setup: Under the grow light 10-14 in away for 12 h a day, or a bright east window. Humidity 50% or more. It can be given a small pole to climb as it grows.
plants.water_notes: In this chunky, airy mix, water when the top is dry and the pot feels light, soaking through and draining fully. Roughly weekly under the light in summer, every 10-14 days in winter. Yellow lower leaves usually mean too wet; crispy edges, too dry or too dry an air.
plants.soil_medium: Chunky aroid mix: bark, lava rock or pumice, perlite and a little coco coir or potting soil. The current mix of lava rock and bark is right.
plants.nutrients: Light, regular feeding in the growing season; flush the mix every couple of months.
plants.pests_watch:
Spider mites: stippled leaves and fine webbing in dry air
Thrips: silvery streaks, black specks, deformed new leaves
Mealybugs at the leaf bases
plants.pest_steps:
Check the new leaves and the leaf stalk bases every two weeks.
Wipe the leaves; treat with insecticidal soap or neem if anything is found.
Keep it apart from new plants for two weeks.
plants.height_pot: 1 to 2 ft (slowly to 3 ft or more with a pole)
plants.native_range: A cultivated hybrid; its parents are Philodendron species of tropical Central and South America.
plants.danger_humans: All parts contain calcium oxalate crystals: chewing burns the mouth and throat. The sap can irritate skin.
plants.danger_animals: Toxic to cats and dogs (ASPCA, Philodendron): drooling, mouth pain, vomiting.
plants.propagation: Stem cuttings with a node, or division of a plant with more than one crown, rooted in moist chunky mix or sphagnum.

H-E-B tag on the plant (Philodendron Ring of Fire, 'Philodendron serratum', full sun, foliage)
NC State Extension Plant Toolbox: Philodendron hederaceum | https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/philodendron-hederaceum/
The University of Kansas Health System Poison Control: Philodendron | https://www.kansashealthsystem.com/care/centers/poison-control-center/poisonous-plants/philodendron
ASPCA toxic and non-toxic plants | https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/toxic-and-non-toxic-plants
plants.health_summary: A young plant with a few good variegated leaves and a strong new one opening, but one leaf has dried brown, two lower leaves are pale and limp, and the leaf stalks are long: it is settling in and could use a little more light and a steady watering rhythm.
plants.health_observations:
New leaf opening, well variegated
One lower leaf dried brown
Two pale, thin lower leaves
Long leaf stalks (reaching for light)
Chunky lava and bark mix, good drainage
Under a grow light, with humidity meters reading about 65%
plants.health_steps:
Cut off the dried leaf at the base.
Bring the grow light a little closer, or lengthen its hours to 12.
Water only when the pot feels light; let it drain fully.
Start half-strength feeding in March.

plants.common_name: Monstera 'Thai Constellation' (left of the pole, speckled leaves)
plants.aliases: Tag: H-E-B 'Monstera Thai Constellation, Monstera deliciosa'; Swiss cheese plant (variegated); 'Thai Constellation' left plant
plants.location: Indoors, on the plant table under the grow light, sharing a pot with the other Thai Constellation
plants.container: Grey plastic pot on a terracotta saucer, sphagnum moss and bark with lava rock, a plastic-mesh moss pole shared by both plants; H-E-B tag
plants.pot_size: Medium: fits in a big tub
plants.growth_habit: A climbing aroid: heart-shaped juvenile leaves now, splits and holes (fenestrations) once it climbs; the cream variegation is stable (tissue-culture)
plants.id_basis: The H-E-B tag reads 'Monstera Thai Constellation, Monstera deliciosa', and the leaves match: heart-shaped juvenile Monstera leaves speckled and splashed with cream, on a moss pole in sphagnum. 'Thai Constellation' is the tissue-cultured variegated form of Monstera deliciosa with stable cream speckling.
plants.id_alternatives:
Monstera deliciosa 'Thai Constellation' (as tagged)
Monstera deliciosa 'Albo Variegata' (sectoral white patches, less speckling, unstable)
Monstera deliciosa (plain; no)
plants.id_improve: Nothing needed: the tag and the leaves agree. A photo when the first split leaf opens would be nice for the record.
plants.temp_notes: Tropical: keep it above 55 F. Chilling marks the cream parts first.
plants.humidity_notes: The cream patches brown at the edges in dry air; 55-65% is a good target under the light.
plants.light_summary: Bright indirect light (the cream parts cannot photosynthesise, so it needs more light than a green Monstera, but no hot sun)
plants.light_hours: 6-8 h bright indirect, or a grow light 12 h
plants.light_notes: The tag's 'full sun' is nursery shade-house advice. Indoors, direct midday sun scorches the cream areas (the browning on the palest leaf). Too little light gives small, slow leaves.
plants.winter_summary: A tropical aroid: indoors all year in Round Rock, under the grow light in winter.
plants.winter_triggers: Already indoors; keep it above 60 F and away from cold glass.
plants.winter_steps:
Grow light 12 h a day.
Let the sphagnum dry on top before watering; water less from November to February.
No feeding in winter.
Keep the moss pole damp so the aerial roots take hold.
plants.indoor_setup: Under the grow light 12-18 in away for 12 h, or a bright east or north-east window. Humidity 50% or more. Tie new growth to the pole as it climbs: leaves get bigger and split sooner.
plants.water_notes: Water when the top inch of sphagnum is dry and the pot is light, soaking through and draining the saucer. Roughly weekly in summer under the light, every 10-14 days in winter. Sphagnum holds a lot of water: the main risk is keeping it wet. Yellow leaves with soft stems mean too wet.
plants.soil_medium: Chunky aroid mix: bark, perlite or pumice, a little coco coir or sphagnum. The current sphagnum and lava rock works if it is allowed to dry between waterings.
plants.nutrients: Regular light feeding; the plant grows slowly and burns with strong feed.
plants.pests_watch:
Thrips: silvery streaks and black specks, deformed new leaves (common on variegated Monstera)
Spider mites: stippling and webbing in dry air
Scale and mealybugs at the leaf stalk bases
plants.pest_steps:
Check both sides of each leaf and the stalk bases every two weeks, with a torch.
Wipe leaves; treat thrips with spinosad or insecticidal soap and repeat weekly for a month.
Quarantine new plants.
plants.height_pot: 2 to 3 ft now; 6 ft and more on a pole
plants.native_range: The species is from southern Mexico to Panama (rain forest climber); this cultivar came from a Thai tissue-culture lab.
plants.conservation_status: Not applicable: a cultivar; the species is widespread.
plants.invasive: Not a risk here (invasive in some tropical islands).
plants.bloom: Rare indoors (a creamy spathe on a mature plant).
plants.fruit: The edible "fruit salad" fruit of the species, on mature outdoor plants only; unripe fruit burns the mouth.
plants.danger_humans: Leaves and stems contain calcium oxalate crystals: chewing burns the mouth and throat.
plants.danger_animals: Toxic to cats and dogs (ASPCA): drooling, mouth pain, vomiting.
plants.propagation: A stem cutting with a node and an aerial root, rooted in water, sphagnum or perlite. Choose a node whose leaf has both green and cream.
plants.sources:

plants.health_summary: Growing, with fresh juvenile leaves and aerial roots reaching the pole, but several leaves have dried tips and brown patches on the cream areas, and one or two old leaves have died back at the base. Looks like the cream parts have scorched or dried in low humidity, and the sphagnum has been kept fairly wet.
plants.health_observations:
Juvenile heart-shaped leaves, no splits yet
Cream areas browning on the palest leaf
Dried leaf tips and one dead leaf at the base
Aerial roots growing into the shared moss pole
Sphagnum and lava rock, pot on a saucer under the grow light
plants.health_steps:
Cut off the dead leaf and trim the brown tips with clean scissors, leaving a thin brown margin.
Move the grow light a little further (18 in) or shorten its hours if the cream patches keep browning.
Let the sphagnum dry on top between waterings; empty the saucer.
Raise humidity around the table in winter.
Pot the two plants separately in spring if either is to grow large: they will compete for the one pole.

plants.aliases: Tag: H-E-B 'Monstera Thai Constellation, Monstera deliciosa'; Swiss cheese plant (variegated); 'Thai Constellation' right plant
plants.location: Indoors, on the plant table under the grow light, sharing a pot with the other Thai Constellation
plants.container: Grey plastic pot on a terracotta saucer, sphagnum moss and bark with lava rock, a plastic-mesh moss pole shared by both plants; H-E-B tag
plants.pot_size: Medium: fits in a big tub
plants.growth_habit: A climbing aroid: heart-shaped juvenile leaves now, splits and holes (fenestrations) once it climbs; the cream variegation is stable (tissue-culture)
plants.id_basis: The H-E-B tag reads 'Monstera Thai Constellation, Monstera deliciosa', and the leaves match: heart-shaped juvenile Monstera leaves speckled and splashed with cream, on a moss pole in sphagnum. 'Thai Constellation' is the tissue-cultured variegated form of Monstera deliciosa with stable cream speckling.
plants.id_alternatives:
Monstera deliciosa 'Thai Constellation' (as tagged)
Monstera deliciosa 'Albo Variegata' (sectoral white patches, less speckling, unstable)
Monstera deliciosa (plain; no)
plants.id_improve: Nothing needed: the tag and the leaves agree. A photo when the first split leaf opens would be nice for the record.
plants.temp_notes: Tropical: keep it above 55 F. Chilling marks the cream parts first.
plants.humidity_notes: The cream patches brown at the edges in dry air; 55-65% is a good target under the light.
plants.light_summary: Bright indirect light (the cream parts cannot photosynthesise, so it needs more light than a green Monstera, but no hot sun)
plants.light_hours: 6-8 h bright indirect, or a grow light 12 h
plants.light_notes: The tag's 'full sun' is nursery shade-house advice. Indoors, direct midday sun scorches the cream areas (the browning on the palest leaf). Too little light gives small, slow leaves.
plants.winter_summary: A tropical aroid: indoors all year in Round Rock, under the grow light in winter.
plants.winter_triggers: Already indoors; keep it above 60 F and away from cold glass.
plants.winter_steps:
Grow light 12 h a day.
Let the sphagnum dry on top before watering; water less from November to February.
No feeding in winter.
Keep the moss pole damp so the aerial roots take hold.
plants.indoor_setup: Under the grow light 12-18 in away for 12 h, or a bright east or north-east window. Humidity 50% or more. Tie new growth to the pole as it climbs: leaves get bigger and split sooner.
plants.water_notes: Water when the top inch of sphagnum is dry and the pot is light, soaking through and draining the saucer. Roughly weekly in summer under the light, every 10-14 days in winter. Sphagnum holds a lot of water: the main risk is keeping it wet. Yellow leaves with soft stems mean too wet.
plants.soil_medium: Chunky aroid mix: bark, perlite or pumice, a little coco coir or sphagnum. The current sphagnum and lava rock works if it is allowed to dry between waterings.
plants.nutrients: Regular light feeding; the plant grows slowly and burns with strong feed.
plants.pests_watch:
Thrips: silvery streaks and black specks, deformed new leaves (common on variegated Monstera)
Spider mites: stippling and webbing in dry air
Scale and mealybugs at the leaf stalk bases
plants.pest_steps:
Check both sides of each leaf and the stalk bases every two weeks, with a torch.
Wipe leaves; treat thrips with spinosad or insecticidal soap and repeat weekly for a month.
Quarantine new plants.
plants.height_pot: 2 to 3 ft now; 6 ft and more on a pole
plants.native_range: The species is from southern Mexico to Panama (rain forest climber); this cultivar came from a Thai tissue-culture lab.
plants.conservation_status: Not applicable: a cultivar; the species is widespread.
plants.invasive: Not a risk here (invasive in some tropical islands).
plants.bloom: Rare indoors (a creamy spathe on a mature plant).
plants.fruit: The edible "fruit salad" fruit of the species, on mature outdoor plants only; unripe fruit burns the mouth.
plants.danger_humans: Leaves and stems contain calcium oxalate crystals: chewing burns the mouth and throat.
plants.danger_animals: Toxic to cats and dogs (ASPCA): drooling, mouth pain, vomiting.
plants.propagation: A stem cutting with a node and an aerial root, rooted in water, sphagnum or perlite. Choose a node whose leaf has both green and cream.

Spider mites: silvery pitting on the leaf undersides

Look into the leaf axils and along the leaf undersides every week.
Dab mealybugs with rubbing alcohol on a cotton bud, then spray the whole plant (axils, undersides, the top of the medium) with insecticidal soap or 70% alcohol, repeating every 5-7 days for three weeks.

plants.id_basis: The Costa Farms tag says Flame Violet / Episcia cupreata, and the plant matches: rounded, quilted, velvety leaves in copper, bronze and pale green with a lighter midrib, spreading by runners, a dead flower stalk still on it. This is the larger clump with the copper colouring.
plants.id_alternatives:
Episcia cupreata (as tagged)
Episcia 'Silver Skies' or another silver-leaved cultivar
plants.id_improve: A photo of a flower when it blooms (colour and fringing name the cultivar).
plants.health_summary: Several healthy quilted leaves and runners, but the leaf edges are curling and browning and some leaves are dull: dry air and probably cold water on the leaves. The bowl mix looks dry on top.
plants.health_observations:
Copper-bronze quilted leaves, pale midribs
Leaf edges curling and browning
A spent flower stalk
Runners spreading over the mix
plants.health_steps:
Raise the humidity: a cloche or a terrarium, or a humid grouping under the light.
Water at the soil with room-temperature water; keep the leaves dry.
Cut the dead flower stalk off.
In spring, move it (and its runners) to a shallow pot of its own: the Gynura will shade it out.

plants.growth_habit: A low, creeping gesneriad spreading by runners (stolons), with velvety, quilted leaves; red or orange tubular flowers
plants.temp_notes: Tag: keep above 50 F. It sulks and spots below 60 F; truly tropical.
plants.humidity_notes: Wants humid air: the tag says 'ideal for terrariums'. Edges brown and leaves curl in dry rooms.
plants.light_hours: 4-6 h bright indirect, or a grow light 12 h
plants.light_notes: Tag: bright, tolerates medium. No direct sun on the velvet leaves. Good light brings the copper and silver colour and the flowers.
plants.winter_steps:
Keep it warm (above 60 F) and the air humid: a cloche, a terrarium or a humid corner under the light.
Water with room-temperature water only.
No feeding in winter.
plants.indoor_setup: Under the grow light or in an east window, in a humid group or a terrarium. Water from below or at the soil so the fuzzy leaves stay dry.
plants.water_notes: Tag: weekly. Keep the mix evenly moist but never soggy; water at the soil with room-temperature water (cold water spots the leaves). Let the top half-inch dry between waterings.
plants.soil_medium: Light, airy African-violet mix: peat, perlite and vermiculite.
plants.fertilizer: African-violet feed at quarter strength with every other watering
plants.pests_watch:
Mealybugs in the leaf axils and on runners
Aphids on new growth
Crown rot from cold, wet soil
plants.pest_steps:
Look into the crown and along the runners every two weeks.
Dab mealybugs with rubbing alcohol; keep the crown dry.
plants.lifespan: A few years; runners make new plants
plants.native_range: Northern South America (Colombia, Venezuela, Brazil), on the shaded, humid forest floor.
plants.bloom: Red-orange tubular flowers with fringed edges, on and off through the warm months in good light.
plants.danger_humans: Not known to be toxic; the tag says not for consumption.
plants.danger_animals: Not on the ASPCA toxic lists (African-violet relatives are non-toxic).
plants.propagation: Pin a runner plantlet onto moist mix until it roots, then cut it free; leaf cuttings also work.

plants.aliases: Painted-leaf begonia; the small silver plant at the edge of the bowl
plants.growth_habit: A rhizomatous begonia: a creeping rhizome at the soil surface sending up lopsided, patterned leaves on short red stalks
plants.id_basis: A very small plant with lopsided, rounded leaves patterned silver over dark green with dark veins and a red leaf stalk: a rex (painted-leaf) begonia, the silver-and-green type. It has no tag; the pattern and the leaf shape say Begonia rex-cultorum, but at this size the cultivar cannot be named.
plants.id_alternatives:
Begonia rex-cultorum (silver type, e.g. 'Silver Queen' or 'Escargot' seedling)
Begonia 'Fireflush' type
Peperomia caperata (no: the leaves are lopsided and not deeply corrugated)
plants.id_improve:
A photo once it has a few grown leaves
Where it came from (a cutting, or a plantlet that arrived in the bowl?)
plants.temp_notes: Keep it above 60 F; cold and wet together rot the rhizome.
plants.humidity_notes: Likes humid air but needs air movement; damp, still air brings powdery mildew.
plants.light_hours: 4-6 h bright indirect, or a grow light 12 h
plants.light_notes: No direct sun; the silver patterning is best in bright shade.
plants.winter_steps:
Keep it warm and lightly moist; rex begonias can go partly dormant and drop leaves in winter, growing back from the rhizome in spring.
No feeding in winter.
plants.indoor_setup: Under the grow light or in an east window, in a humid spot with some air movement. A shallow pot of its own once it has a few leaves.
plants.water_notes: Water when the top half-inch is dry, at the soil; keep the leaves and the rhizome dry. Never soggy.
plants.pests_watch:
Powdery mildew (white dust on the leaves) in still, damp air
Mealybugs at the leaf bases
Thrips on new leaves
plants.pest_steps:
Give it air movement and keep the leaves dry.
Remove mildewed leaves; dab mealybugs with rubbing alcohol.
plants.lifespan: A few years; renew from leaf or rhizome cuttings
plants.native_range: Hybrids descended from Begonia rex of north-east India and Assam, with other Asian species.
plants.bloom: Small pink flowers, insignificant; grown for the leaves.
plants.danger_humans: Not known to harm people from handling; the roots and tubers contain soluble oxalates.
plants.danger_animals: Toxic to cats and dogs (ASPCA, Begonia): the underground parts most of all; vomiting and drooling.
plants.propagation: Leaf cuttings laid on moist mix, or a piece of rhizome with a growing point.
